The maps they had were old, drawn by surveyors who had not crossed the river, and the local guides disagreed about which valley led toward the pass. For three days the weather held. On the fourth, snow began to fall in thick, wet flakes, and the mules refused to move until the trail was cleared. The leader ordered the party to camp beside a frozen stream; they spent a miserable night huddled under canvas and the wind tore at the guy ropes.

By morning two of the porters had frostbitten fingers, and the doctor insisted they turn back. The leader refused. He argued that the pass was a day away at most and that a retreat now would waste the supplies they had already consumed. The guides warned that the snow was deepening and that avalanches had killed men on this route before. Nevertheless, the party pressed on, roping themselves together and breaking a trail through drifts that reached their waists. Progress slowed to a few hundred yards an hour.

Around midday the clouds lifted long enough to reveal the ridge they had been aiming for. It looked close, perhaps half a mile distant, but the intervening slope was steep and studded with loose rock. Two men went ahead to scout a line, and the rest waited in the shelter of a boulder. The scouts returned at dusk and reported that the ridge could be climbed, at some risk, and that the far side appeared to drop away into a forest.

That night the temperature fell below zero. The stove would not light, and the men ate cold rations in silence. Some of them, I learned later, had begun to fear that they would see the village again. In fact, the expedition very nearly ended there: a lantern tipped over in the tent, and the quick action of the youngest porter prevented the canvas from catching fire.
